104.t: Being a woman pianist in jazz
104.s: She says it was never an uphill struggle, recalls Leonard Feather's review and other women on the scene.
104.q: I don’t think it was ever an uphill struggle for me, because I sort of had my indoctrination in working with Jimmy and boy Jimmy was so supportive and proud of me. 104.t: Competing as a woman and her low confidence before coming to the States
104.s: She says competition with men was not an issue until she played with Jimmy, who supported her; she knew of Mary Lou Williams, Hazel Scott and Cleo Brown but never went to hear Fats Waller and was just happy to work.
104.ch: Jazz records, vaudeville and starting out
104.q: I don’t think I had any of this until I had come here and done a certain amount of playing with Jimmy. I think to begin with I really hadn’t thought about doing anything. Some people think that I was guilty of some kind of skullduggery, because I married Jimmy. They all thought I wanted to come to…

531.t: Did the women's quintet share that feeling
531.s: She did, but the band never discussed it; there was little awareness then.
531.q: I cannot speak for the others, I certainly did, and we didn’t talk about any of this at that time. There was really no, or very, very little awareness of that in the scene. This has really, really changed now. Everything’s become a lot more open and people talk about it. But at the time I felt the…

531.t: Being the first woman in the WDR Big Band
531.s: Her 2004 vote-based hiring drew sensationalist media interest in what it was like to be the only woman.
531.q: Yes. It was quite a big — I don’t want to say uproar — but there was a lot of media interest because none of the German radio or European radio big band had a female member at the time. This was 2004 when I joined. And yes, it was kind of strange. It was a little bit similar to I don’t know if you…

736.t: Mary Lou Williams and being a woman in jazz
736.s: Williams did not blame being a woman for setbacks, but was labeled a girl pianist and said to play like a man.
736.ch: Mary Lou Williams and Ken Burns
736.q: Yeah. She never — she never felt, from what I’ve read, that being a woman held her back. Whether I agree with that is one thing. But she once said, she once compared herself, she always thought of herself as being just as fine a musician as one of the guys. She knew her art. And so she never…

397.t: Stereotyped as a Latino percussionist, not a straight-ahead player
397.s: He describes being boxed in as a conga or timbales player, which limits work on his own projects; Rowe praises his trio album.
397.q: Yeah it has been that way, especially with the people in the industry. 791.s: Women's festivals gave exposure in the early 70s, but business acceptance has improved less than hoped.

1032.t: Women in jazz, Maqueque and Terri Lyne Carrington
1032.s: She discusses the state of women in jazz, the DownBeat quote on Maqueque, difficult experiences and visa obstacles for her band.
1032.ch: Women in jazz and being Canadian
1032.q: Well I feel great. If there’s a festival it’s a women’s festival that I’m playing at it. If it’s a women’s festival and I’m not playing at it I hate it.

1035.s: Asked whether it matters being a woman, she says playing with another woman feels different and harder.
1035.q: I don’t know. But even playing with a woman is different. I don’t know why. And always the band member is a man, right? But sometimes with a woman I feel different attitude to men, you know, the attitude. And the woman musicians I feel are different.

942.t: Women in jazz and the boy's club
942.s: She discusses persistent male dominance in jazz, programming, tokenism, and her own choice to build her own band rather than play second alto.
942.q: I have very mixed feelings about the word “progressing” with it. But there are some great things that are coming out. There’ve always been some great things. 341.s: In grad school she never thought of hiring women and shared the stereotype; now Diva has few substitutes available.

992.t: Being a woman jazz musician and Me Too
992.s: She discusses tokenism, her mixed feelings on current movements, and the tassel joke.
992.q: Well I have mixed feelings about all these movements about you know women. Because yes we have been discriminated for a long time. 751.t: State of women in jazz today
751.s: Responding to Karolina Strassmayer's quote, Rowe says things are improving, with more young women and record Sisters in Jazz applicants, though not level.
751.q: Well of course needless to say I think about this constantly, you know especially with trying to get a lot of young women in our program which we’ve been, I’ll say I’ve been pretty good at.
